AI in measurement: A reading list

Source: vignettes/articles/ai-reading.Rmd
ai-reading.Rmd

This list is a starting point for a psychometrician who wants to read about artificial intelligence (AI) in testing. Each entry says in one or two sentences why it is worth your time. Entries are grouped in the order of the AI Hub learning path, and the first group is the place to start. Links point to the publisher’s page or a free copy where one exists.

The field moves quickly: This list was checked in November 2026. To suggest an addition, open an issue on GitHub.

Start here: Overviews

  • Bulut, O., Beiting-Parrish, M., Casabianca, J. M., Slater, S. C., Jiao, H., Song, D., Ormerod, C. M., Fabiyi, D. G., Ivan, R., Walsh, C., Rios, O., Wilson, J., Yildirim-Erbasli, S. N., Wongvorachan, T., Liu, J. X., Tan, B., & Morilova, P. (2024). The rise of artificial intelligence in educational measurement: Opportunities and ethical challenges. Chinese/English Journal of Educational Measurement and Evaluation. doi:10.59863/MIQL7785 (preprint).
    A broad survey of where AI is used in testing, from item writing to scoring and reporting, with the validity, fairness and privacy questions each use raises.
  • Hao, J., von Davier, A. A., Yaneva, V., Lottridge, S., von Davier, M., & Harris, D. J. (2024). Transforming assessment: The impacts and implications of large language models and generative AI. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 43(2), 16–29. doi:10.1111/emip.12602
    A short, practical account by testing-industry researchers of what large language models change in item development, scoring and score reporting.
  • von Davier, A. A., Mislevy, R. J., & Hao, J. (Eds.). (2021). Computational psychometrics: New methodologies for a new generation of digital learning and assessment. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-74394-9
    How psychometric models and machine learning combine for data from games, simulations and process logs.

Machine learning through a psychometric lens

  • Breiman, L. (2001). Statistical modeling: The two cultures. Statistical Science, 16(3), 199–231. doi:10.1214/ss/1009213726
    The classic essay on modelling to explain versus modelling to predict. Psychometrics lives mostly in the first culture; this explains the second.
  • Yarkoni, T., & Westfall, J. (2017). Choosing prediction over explanation in psychology: Lessons from machine learning. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 12(6), 1100–1122. doi:10.1177/1745691617693393
    Overfitting, cross-validation and regularization, explained for researchers trained in classical statistics.
  • James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2021). An introduction to statistical learning with applications in R (2nd ed.). Springer. Free PDF
    The standard first textbook, with R labs. Chapters 2, 5 and 6 cover most of what the translation table refers to.

Automated scoring

  • Williamson, D. M., Xi, X., & Breyer, F. J. (2012). A framework for evaluation and use of automated scoring. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 31(1), 2–13. doi:10.1111/j.1745-3992.2011.00223.x
    The source of the agreement thresholds (QWK, standardized mean difference) that score_open() uses. Read this before any scoring project.
  • Yan, D., Rupp, A. A., & Foltz, P. W. (Eds.). (2020). Handbook of automated scoring: Theory into practice. CRC Press.
    The reference book: Scoring engines, evaluation, operational use and validity.
  • Loukina, A., Madnani, N., Cahill, A., Yao, L., Johnson, M. S., Riordan, B., & McCaffrey, D. F. (2020). Using PRMSE to evaluate automated scoring systems in the presence of label noise. In Proceedings of the Fifteenth Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (pp. 18–29). ACL Anthology
    Why agreement with a single human rater undersells a good engine, and how PRMSE corrects for rater error.
  • Bridgeman, B., Trapani, C., & Attali, Y. (2012). Comparison of human and machine scoring of essays: Differences by gender, ethnicity, and country. Applied Measurement in Education, 25(1), 27–40. doi:10.1080/08957347.2012.635502
    An early and clear demonstration that an engine can agree well with humans overall and still score some groups differently.

What item text tells us: Difficulty prediction

  • Fischer, G. H. (1973). The linear logistic test model as an instrument in educational research. Acta Psychologica, 37(6), 359–374. doi:10.1016/0001-6918(73)90003-6
    The psychometric ancestor of difficulty prediction: Item difficulty as a sum of the cognitive operations an item requires.
  • De Boeck, P., & Wilson, M. (Eds.). (2004). Explanatory item response models: A generalized linear and nonlinear approach. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3990-9
    IRT models with item and person covariates, the bridge between features and item parameters.
  • Bulut, O., Gorgun, G., & Yildirim-Erbasli, S. N. (2021). Estimating explanatory extensions of dichotomous and polytomous Rasch models: The eirm package in R. Psych, 3(3), 308–321. doi:10.3390/psych3030023
    Explanatory IRT as generalized linear mixed models in R, with item and person covariates and random item effects.
  • AlKhuzaey, S., Grasso, F., Payne, T. R., & Tamma, V. (2024). Text-based question difficulty prediction: A systematic review of automatic approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34(3), 862–914. doi:10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1
    What features and models have been tried, and how well they work.
  • Benedetto, L., Cremonesi, P., Caines, A., Buttery, P., Cappelli, A., Giussani, A., & Turrin, R. (2023). A survey on recent approaches to question difficulty estimation from text. ACM Computing Surveys, 55(9), Article 178. doi:10.1145/3556538
    A companion survey from the computer science side, including neural approaches.
  • Yaneva, V., North, K., Baldwin, P., Ha, L. A., Rezayi, S., Zhou, Y., Ray Choudhury, S., Harik, P., & Clauser, B. (2024). Findings from the first shared task on automated prediction of difficulty and response time for multiple-choice questions. In Proceedings of the 19th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (pp. 470–482). ACL Anthology
    A sobering benchmark on real licensing-exam items: Many teams, modest gains over a simple baseline.

Automatic item generation

  • Gierl, M. J., & Haladyna, T. M. (Eds.). (2013). Automatic item generation: Theory and practice. Routledge.
    The foundational book on cognitive models, item models and the psychometrics of generated items.
  • Gierl, M. J., & Lai, H. (2013). Instructional topics in educational measurement (ITEMS) module: Using automated processes to generate test items. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 32(3), 36–50. doi:10.1111/emip.12018
    A short teaching module on the three-step method: Cognitive model, item model, generation.
  • Glas, C. A. W., & van der Linden, W. J. (2003). Computerized adaptive testing with item cloning. Applied Psychological Measurement, 27(4), 247–261. doi:10.1177/0146621603027004001
    How to calibrate item families instead of single items, so generated isomorphs can be used without each one being field tested.
  • Sinharay, S., Johnson, M. S., & Williamson, D. M. (2003). Calibrating item families and summarizing the results using family expected response functions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 28(4), 295–313.
    A hierarchical model for item families, with a way to report a family as a whole.
  • Geerlings, H., Glas, C. A. W., & van der Linden, W. J. (2011). Modeling rule-based item generation. Psychometrika, 76(2), 337–359. doi:10.1007/s11336-011-9204-x
    Explains family difficulties by the rules used to generate the items: The LLTM idea applied to item models. In mirtverse: calibrate_families(), the book’s chapter Generating items and Lab 9.
  • von Davier, M. (2018). Automated item generation with recurrent neural networks. Psychometrika, 83(4), 847–857. doi:10.1007/s11336-018-9608-y
    An early neural approach to writing items, before today’s large language models.
  • Circi, R., Hicks, J., & Sikali, E. (2023). Automatic item generation: Foundations and machine learning-based approaches for assessments. Frontiers in Education, 8, 858273. doi:10.3389/feduc.2023.858273
    A review that places template and machine learning approaches side by side.

Language models as respondents

  • Argyle, L. P., Busby, E. C., Fulda, N., Gubler, J. R., Rytting, C., & Wingate, D. (2023). Out of one, many: Using language models to simulate human samples. Political Analysis, 31(3), 337–351. doi:10.1017/pan.2023.2
    The paper that started the “silicon sample” debate. Read it alongside a psychometric check of whether simulated responses behave like real ones, such as the one in the box on simulated respondents in the book’s chapter on large language models (with simulate_llm_respondents() and compare_synthetic(), which are experimental). To see where synthetic respondents land in the real population, use the coverage strip in Checking synthetic respondents.

Validity, fairness and governance

  • American Educational Research Association, American Psychological Association, & National Council on Measurement in Education. (2014). Standards for educational and psychological testing. AERA. Free PDF
    Not about AI, but every AI use in testing is ultimately judged against it.
  • Kane, M. T. (2013). Validating the interpretations and uses of test scores. Journal of Educational Measurement, 50(1), 1–73. doi:10.1111/jedm.12000
    The argument-based approach to validity, which gives a structure for asking what an AI component must be shown to do.
  • Johnson, M. S., Liu, X., & McCaffrey, D. F. (2022). Psychometric methods to evaluate measurement and algorithmic bias in automated scoring. Journal of Educational Measurement, 59(3), 338–361. doi:10.1111/jedm.12335
    Separates bias in what the engine measures from bias in how it predicts, using tools a psychometrician already knows. In mirtverse: The differential scoring check of ai_audit(), the book’s chapter Validity, fairness and governance of AI and Lab 10.
  • International Test Commission & Association of Test Publishers. (2022). Guidelines for technology-based assessment.
    Practical guidance on scoring, security, accessibility and fairness for computer-delivered tests, including automated scoring.
